ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Thirty blows is a fixed counted beating assigned as a public verdict in Chan encounters and later comments.
EvidenceBody: The sentence can arrive before action: Kaixian says it is due before crossing the teaching-hall gate, Dahui quotes its being due before stepping onto a boat, and Baoning makes movement itself incur it. It can also be retrospective or directed upward: Xuedou assigns it before Huineng reaches Caoxi, Nanjian has thirty blows for the World-Honored One, and Fohri Xi refuses to spare even one blow from earlier commentators. “I let you off with thirty blows” makes the sentence itself a pointed form of leniency in Jian Shan and Qingxi. Zen bends a conventional counted beating into a reusable teaching-seat judgement whose recipient may be monk, commentator, patriarch, or buddha.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: A counted corporal sentence becomes a portable public verdict, including paradoxical formulas in which thirty blows are what “letting off” means.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The phrase names the assigned blows, not a universal explanation of why each recipient deserves them; each surrounding exchange supplies the charge.
